examples: The witness was adjured to answer truthfully or not at all.
He adjured them to remember what the founders had risked.
The high priest adjured him to say whether the charge was true.
In the last paragraph she adjures her readers to check the primary sources themselves.
Nobody had adjured me to secrecy; I simply kept quiet.
She adjured him by the memory of his mother not to sell the farm.
entries.русский: заклинать — торжественно требовать во имя святого или под клятвой; книжн., устар.
entries.patterns: adjure + sb + to-infinitive · adjure + sb + that-clause (archaic) · adjure + sb + by + noun phrase (adjured him by all he held sacred)
entries.never: adjure someone from doing something — the from + -ing frame belongs to prohibit and bar. adjure to do something with no object is also impossible: somebody is always being sworn.
entries.reports: a command laid on someone under oath or in the name of something sacred — it sits between command and implore and carries an appeal to conscience that neither of its neighbors has. Unlike a plain order, it presumes the hearer wants to do right.

examples: My parents never allowed us to eat in the living room.
The airline allows one carry-on and one personal item.
Her visa allowed her to stay another ninety days.
The building doesn't allow subletting under any circumstances.
The judge allowed the question, over the objection.
I'll allow that the timing looks bad, but nothing was hidden.
entries.русский: разрешать, позволять — просто не возражать; слабее permit и authorize
entries.patterns: allow + sb + to-infinitive · allow + -ing (no person named: allows smoking) · allow + noun phrase · allow + sb + noun phrase (allowed us ten minutes) · passive be allowed to (very common) · allow for + noun phrase (= make room for, a different verb: allow for traffic) · allow + that-clause (a different verb — see below)
entries.never: allow that you park here as a grant of permission. Permission never takes a that-clause in English. Repairs: allows you to park here, allows parking here. And allow someone doing something — the gerund frame drops the person entirely.
entries.two verbs: allow + that-clause is a concession, not a permission — I'll allow that he had a point means "I concede." It reports agreement, not authorization, and it does not take the subjunctive: allow that he had a point, not have.
entries.reports: permission as the withdrawal of an objection — weaker than permit, which is institutional, and than authorize, which requires someone with formal power. Its negative is the everyday way English forbids things: They don't allow dogs in here.

examples: The mayor appealed to residents to conserve water through the weekend.
Aid groups have appealed for another forty million dollars.
She appealed to her brother for help with the mortgage.
Both sides appealed to the union to return to the table.
He appealed to the crowd's better instincts and got nowhere.
The family appealed to anyone with information to call the tip line.
entries.русский: обращаться с призывом к — публично просить тех, кто не обязан подчиняться
entries.patterns: appeal to + sb + to-infinitive · appeal to + sb + for + noun phrase · appeal for + noun phrase (no addressee named) · appeal to + sb (bare: appealed to the crowd)
entries.never: appeal someone to do something — the preposition to is not optional before the person. Repairs: appealed to him to come forward, or switch verbs: urged him to come forward.
entries.american note: in the courtroom sense, American English makes appeal transitive — she appealed the ruling. British English keeps the preposition — appealed against the ruling. In American writing, ✗ appealed against the verdict reads as an import.
entries.reports: an urgent request broadcast to people who are under no obligation to comply — the verb of press conferences, open letters, and relief campaigns. It has no authority behind it at all, which is exactly what distinguishes it from demand and call on.
entries.see also: call on, urge, plead, beg, petition

examples: He asked me to water his plants while he was in Tulsa.
She asked to speak to whoever was in charge.
I asked the waiter for a glass of tap water.
We ask that all phones be silenced during the performance.
Nobody asked him to do any of this.
She asked whether the position was still open.
entries.русский: просить — нейтральная просьба без оттенков; в другом значении «спрашивать»
entries.type: reporting verb — request (also the neutral question verb)
entries.patterns: ask + sb + to-infinitive · ask + to-infinitive (the subject acts) · ask + (sb) + for + noun phrase · ask + that-clause (subjunctive; formal) · ask + sb + wh-clause · ask + sb + if/whether-clause · ask + sb + noun phrase (asked me a question) · ask + sb + about + noun phrase
entries.never: ask to someone to do something — the addressee takes no preposition. And ask for to do something — for introduces a noun, never an infinitive: asked for the check, not ✗ asked for to see the check.
entries.the object flips the subject: this is the one thing about ask that must be right. She asked to leave means she leaves; She asked me to leave means I do. No other verb in this file makes the distinction so cheaply.
entries.reports: the unmarked request — neutral in force, neutral in register, and silent about how politely the original was phrased. "Close the window," "Could you close the window?" and "I hate to ask, but would it be possible to close the window?" all come out as She asked me to close the window; if the manner mattered, use an adverb or a stronger verb.

examples: Congress authorized the agency to issue subpoenas.
Only two people are authorized to sign checks over ten thousand dollars.
Her supervisor authorized the overtime in writing.
Nobody authorized this purchase, and now it's on the audit.
The warrant authorized them to search the garage but not the house.
I'm not authorized to discuss an open investigation.
entries.русский: уполномочивать, санкционировать — давать право властью должности; офиц.
entries.patterns: authorize + sb + to-infinitive · authorize + noun phrase (authorized the payment) · passive be authorized to (very common)
entries.never: authorize to release the funds with nothing in between — authorize always takes an object, either the person empowered or the thing approved. And authorize someone doing something — no gerund frame.
entries.spelling: American English writes authorize, always. Authorise is the British and Commonwealth spelling — a dialect variant rather than an error, and note that Oxford British style prefers -ize too. In American prose, write authorize.
entries.reports: permission conferred by someone whose office gives them the power to confer it. allow removes an objection; authorize creates a right, and it implies a record — a signature, a resolution, a memo. Its passive is where it lives: You are not authorized to be in this room.

examples: Several states have banned the sale of flavored vaping products.
The league banned him for the rest of the season.
Our building banned smoking on the balconies in 2019.
The country banned imports of beef from three provinces.
She was banned from the online forum for a week.
You can't ban a book from a public library that easily.
entries.русский: запрещать — официальный запрет деятельности властью или организацией
entries.patterns: ban + noun phrase · ban + -ing · ban + sb + from + -ing · ban + sb + from + noun phrase (banned him from the building)
entries.never: ban someone to do something — there is no infinitive frame at all. Repairs: banned him from driving, banned driving, banned drivers from using phones.
entries.reports: the suppression of an activity by a government, an institution, or a governing body — the activity is the target, and the people affected are whoever happens to be doing it. Contrast bar, which targets a person, and forbid, which is what one person says to another.

examples: The state barred him from practicing medicine for five years.
Security barred us from the loading dock without a badge.
A conflict of interest bars her from voting on the measure.
Nothing in the lease bars tenants from keeping a cat.
The court held that the settlement barred any further claims.
He was barred from the building the same afternoon he was fired.
entries.русский: не допускать, отстранять — запрет, закрывающий доступ конкретному человеку; юр.
entries.patterns: bar + sb + from + -ing · bar + sb + from + noun phrase · bar + noun phrase (legal: the statute bars recovery)
entries.never: bar someone to do something, and bar someone doing something without from. The preposition is obligatory whenever a person is named.
entries.reports: prohibition achieved by shutting someone out — of a place, an office, a profession, a remedy. ban abolishes an activity; bar excludes a person from it. In legal writing it is also the verb for a rule that forecloses a claim: The statute of limitations bars the suit.

entries.meaning: The object flips the subject, exactly as with ask: He begged to differ — he differs. He begged me to reconsider — I reconsider.
examples: She begged her landlord to hold the apartment until Friday.
He begged to be excused from the table.
The dog begs for scraps every single night.
I begged him not to put it in writing.
They begged the committee for one more hearing.
I beg to differ with almost everything in that paragraph.
entries.русский: умолять, упрашивать — просить от безысходности, не имея никаких рычагов
entries.patterns: beg + sb + to-infinitive · beg + to-infinitive (the subject acts) · beg + (sb) + for + noun phrase · beg + of + sb (formal and dated: I beg of you) · beg + that-clause (subjunctive; literary)
entries.never: beg to someone to do something — no preposition before the person. Compare plead, which requires one.
entries.reports: a request made from need, with the speaker's dignity spent — the bottom of the force scale. Reporting a request as begged is a strong editorial claim about the original: it says the speaker had no leverage.

examples: She beseeched the governor to grant a stay of execution.
In the letter he besought his brother for forgiveness.
We beseech thee, O Lord, to look upon this house.
The ambassador beseeched both capitals to keep the line open.
I beseeched him — half joking, half not — to stop sending me drafts at midnight.
The petition beseeches the council to reconsider the closure.
entries.русский: молить, умолять — книжн., литург.: высокий стиль beg
entries.patterns: beseech + sb + to-infinitive · beseech + sb + for + noun phrase · beseech + that-clause (archaic)
entries.never: beseech to someone — like beg and unlike plead, it takes a bare object. And beseech someone doing something.
entries.past tense: besought and beseeched are both correct. Besought is the older form and still the one in scripture and poetry; beseeched is more common in modern American prose and is what to write if you are not aiming for an archaic effect.
entries.reports: an urgent, humbled plea — beg transposed into a liturgical or high-literary key. Almost nobody uses it of an ordinary conversation; using it of one is a deliberate exaggeration.

examples: The king bade the messenger rise.
She bade us farewell at the platform and did not look back.
He did as he was bidden and asked no questions.
The innkeeper bade them come in out of the rain.
Custom bids us wait until the eldest is seated.
I bid you good night.
entries.русский: велеть, повелеть — устар., книжн.; берёт инфинитив без to (bade her enter)
entries.patterns: bid + sb + bare infinitive (bade her enter) · bid + sb + to-infinitive (older and rarer) · bid + sb + noun phrase (bade them farewell)
entries.never: bid that she leave — in its command sense, modern bid takes no that-clause. And bid to someone to do something.
entries.forms: past bade, pronounced /bæd/ · BAD in traditional American usage, though /beɪd/ · BAYD is widespread and unremarkable. Past participle bidden. The auction and card-game verb is a different word with a regular past — bid, bid.
entries.bare infinitive: bid is one of the very few directive verbs to drop to — He bade her sit down, not ✗ He bade her to sit down in current literary use. The only other verb in this file that does it is let.
entries.reports: a command in a raised, old-fashioned register — the verb of scripture, fairy tales, and historical fiction. In everyday American English it survives mainly in bid farewell and do as you're bidden.

examples: Three senators called on the agency to release the full report.
The union called for a strike vote by the end of the month.
She called upon her colleagues to put the vote off a week.
The editorial calls on the mayor to apologize publicly.
Nobody called for his resignation, but nobody defended him either.
He called on us for a decision before the market opened.
entries.русский: призывать — публично требовать действий от того, кого нельзя принудить
entries.patterns: call on + sb + to-infinitive · call on + sb + for + noun phrase · call for + noun phrase (no addressee: called for calm) · call for + -ing (called for tightening the rules)
entries.never: call someone to resign — without on, the verb means "telephone," and the sentence changes meaning entirely. call on someone doing something is impossible too.
entries.reports: a demand made in public, addressed to someone with the power to act, by someone with no power to compel them. It is the standard verb of resolutions, statements, and editorials. Call upon is the same verb, one register higher.
entries.second sense: call on someone also means to pay a visit, or to invite a student to speak — The professor called on me first. Context separates them without difficulty.
entries.see also: appeal to, urge, demand, press, exhort

entries.meaning: Three verbs wearing one spelling. The complement decides which one you have written, and they are not near neighbors: The middle row is ambiguous outside context — charged him with theft accuses, charged him with the accounts assigns — and only the third row is the accusation verb proper, which never takes a personal object before its clause: ✗ charged him that the company knew.
examples: The judge charged the jurors to disregard the last exchange entirely.
The commission was charged with reviewing every permit issued since 2020.
He charged his successor to finish what the department had started.
She charged us to keep the news to ourselves until Monday.
The task force is charged with producing recommendations by spring.
In his last letter he charged them to look after their mother.
entries.русский: поручать, возлагать обязанность — торжественное наставление; офиц., юр.
entries.type: reporting verb — formal instruction assigning a duty
entries.patterns: charge + sb + to-infinitive · charge + sb + with + -ing (charged him with organizing the drive) · charge + sb + with + noun phrase · passive be charged with (the commonest form) · charge + that-clause (a different verb — see below)
entries.never: charge someone that they do something — the directive verb takes no that-clause, and no personal object may stand in front of one. Repairs: charged him to finish it, charged him with finishing it. And charge someone to do something when you mean accuse: the infinitive frame only ever assigns a duty.
entries.reports: a solemn instruction that hands somebody a responsibility — a judge to a jury, an outgoing officer to a successor, a commencement speaker to a graduating class. It is instruct with ceremony attached.

examples: The captain commanded the crew to stand down.
She commanded him to leave the house and never come back.
The statute commands that every ballot be preserved for twenty-two months.
He does not so much ask as command.
Her work commands respect even from people who disagree with it.
The officer commanded us not to move until the all-clear.
entries.русский: приказывать, повелевать — приказ, ослушаться которого нельзя; воен., книжн.
entries.patterns: command + sb + to-infinitive · command + that-clause (subjunctive) · command + noun phrase (commanded silence)
entries.never: command to advance with no object — somebody must be commanded. And command that he advances — the that-clause takes the bare subjunctive, not the indicative.
entries.subjunctive: command that takes the base form for every subject and never backshifts: He commanded that the gates be shut, never were shut.
entries.second sense: command also means "elicit without asking" — commands respect, commands a high price, commands a view of the harbor. That verb reports nothing at all; it takes only a noun phrase.
entries.reports: the strongest directive in the language — an order from someone whose authority makes refusal a breach of duty. Where order is administrative and can come from a doctor or a court, command is military, royal, or divine, and in ordinary American office English it always sounds like an exaggeration.

examples: The czar decreed that the calendar be changed.
The court decreed that the estate be divided equally among the three children.
Some committee somewhere has decreed that we all use the new template.
In 1685 the king decreed the revocation of the edict.
Nature has not decreed that offices must be cold.
The board decreed that no exceptions be made for anyone.
entries.русский: постановлять, издавать указ — приказ, сразу ставший законом; часто иронично
entries.patterns: decree + that-clause (subjunctive) · decree + noun phrase (decreed a general amnesty)
entries.never: decree someone to do something — decree takes no personal object before a complement. Repairs: decreed that he step down, decreed his removal.
entries.subjunctive: the base form throughout, and no backshift: The emperor decreed that the temple be rebuilt, not was rebuilt.
entries.reports: a command that becomes law the instant it is uttered, issued by an authority answerable to no one. Applied to an ordinary person it is heavily ironic — My sister has decreed that we're doing Thanksgiving at her place.

examples: The union demanded that the layoffs be rescinded.
He demanded to know who had authorized the transfer.
Protesters demanded the release of the detained journalists.
She demanded of him an explanation he was in no position to give.
The tenants demanded that the heat be fixed before the weekend.
Nobody is demanding perfection; we're asking for a deadline.
entries.русский: требовать — настойчиво, не оставляя собеседнику возможности отказать
entries.patterns: demand + that-clause (subjunctive) · demand + to-infinitive (the subject acts: demanded to see the manager) · demand + noun phrase · demand + noun phrase + of + sb (demanded an explanation of him) · demand + of + sb + that-clause (formal)
entries.never: demand someone to do something — one of the highest-frequency errors in this whole file, because demand looks exactly like order and require, both of which accept the object plus infinitive. It does not. Repairs: demanded that he resign, demanded his resignation, demanded to see him.
entries.subjunctive: bare base form, all persons, no backshift. She demanded that he be present, not was present; He demanded that the invoice be paid; negative with plain not — demanded that we not tell the press, never ✗ that we don't tell. British writing has demanded that he should be present, which is a dialect difference and not an error.
entries.the mirror-image error: demand's object-plus-infinitive gap has an exact counterpart worth knowing — want and expect take the object plus infinitive and refuse the that-clause. ✗ I want that you come and ✗ I demanded him to come are the same learner making opposite errors.
entries.reports: a request presented as an entitlement, with no room left for a no. It differs from require in that a person demands and a rule requires, and from insist on in that demand is a single act while insist implies repetition against resistance.
entries.see also: require, insist on, order, request, ask

examples: The larger firm dictated every clause of the merger agreement.
Policy dictates that all incidents be logged within twenty-four hours.
He isn't going to let a subcontractor dictate to him.
Weather dictated the schedule more than anything on the whiteboard did.
The budget dictates how many people we can bring on this year.
She dictated two letters and a memo before nine.
entries.русский: диктовать, навязывать условия — с осуждением: так о себе не говорят
entries.patterns: dictate + that-clause · dictate + noun phrase (dictated the terms) · dictate + noun phrase + to + sb (dictated the terms to them) · dictate + wh-clause (dictates who gets in) · dictate to + sb (intransitive: nobody dictates to me)
entries.never: dictate someone to do something — no object plus infinitive. Repairs: dictated that he step down, dictated the terms of his exit.
entries.mood: the that-clause goes subjunctive when dictate imposes a rule (policy dictates that the form be notarized) and indicative when it merely predicts or explains (common sense dictates that this will take longer). Both are current; the second is far commoner in American writing.
entries.second sense: dictate a letter — speak words for someone else to transcribe. That verb takes only a noun phrase and reports nothing.
entries.reports: terms laid down by whoever is in a position to lay them down, with an unmistakable note of resentment on the reporter's part. Nobody describes their own reasonable instruction as dictating.

examples: The inspector directed us to shut the line down until the guard was replaced.
Her will directs that the proceeds go to the county library.
The memo directed all staff to complete the training by the fifteenth.
The referee directed both coaches to their benches.
He was directed to appear at ten and showed up at noon.
The statute directs the agency to publish its findings annually.
entries.русский: предписывать, распоряжаться — официальное указание по инстанции; юр., корп.
entries.patterns: direct + sb + to-infinitive · direct + that-clause (subjunctive) · direct + sb + to + noun phrase (a different sense: directed us to the elevators)
entries.never: direct someone doing something — no gerund frame. direct to do something with no object is impossible in the directive sense.
entries.subjunctive: direct that takes the base form and does not backshift — The court directed that the exhibits be returned.
entries.reports: an instruction issued through a chain of authority — the verb of court orders, agency letters, and corporate memoranda. It has the force of order without its edge: nobody is being shouted at, but nobody is being asked either.

entries.meaning: The preposition carries the meaning. This is the only verb in the file that points in both directions, and nothing but the preposition tells you which: In modern American English the from sense dominates so completely — it is the verb behind the noun injunction — that a reader meeting enjoined to outside a religious or literary text often has to reread.
examples: A federal judge enjoined the state from enforcing the new rule.
The rule of the order enjoined silence between compline and dawn.
Plaintiffs asked the court to enjoin the merger pending review.
He was enjoined from contacting any former client for two years.
Scripture enjoins believers to care for the widow and the orphan.
The injunction enjoining construction was lifted in March.
entries.русский: предписывать; юр. запрещать судебным решением — совмещает приказ и запрет
entries.patterns: enjoin + sb + to-infinitive (= order them to) · enjoin + sb + from + -ing (= forbid them from) · enjoin + that-clause (subjunctive) · enjoin + noun phrase (enjoined silence, enjoined the merger)
entries.never: enjoin someone doing something without from, and enjoin someone against doing something — the preposition is from.
entries.reports: in law, a binding order of a court, most often one that stops something. In older moral and religious writing, a duty solemnly urged.

examples: The letter entreats the governor to commute the sentence.
She entreated her son to write, even a postcard.
He entreated them for a few more days to find the money.
I entreat you to read the second half before you decide.
The delegation entreated both sides to keep talking.
His mother had entreated him not to enlist, and he enlisted anyway.
entries.русский: умолять, упрашивать — книжн.: горячо, но без отчаяния и потери достоинства
entries.patterns: entreat + sb + to-infinitive · entreat + sb + for + noun phrase · entreat + that-clause (formal, rare)
entries.never: entreat to someone to do something — bare object, no preposition. And entreat someone from doing something.
entries.reports: an earnest and courteous plea — beg with the desperation removed and the manners left in. Where beg implies the speaker has nothing left, entreat implies only that they care very much. It is a written word; almost no American says it aloud.

examples: He exhorted the volunteers to knock on one more door before dark.
The general exhorted his troops to hold the line one more hour.
Her columns exhort readers to vote in local elections nobody follows.
The letter exhorts the churches to stand firm.
She exhorted us to greater discipline and, less usefully, to greater cheerfulness.
Coaches can exhort all they want; the roster is the roster.
entries.русский: призывать, увещевать — книжн.: риторическое воодушевление аудитории
entries.patterns: exhort + sb + to-infinitive · exhort + sb + to + noun phrase (exhorted them to greater effort) · exhort + that-clause (subjunctive; rare)
entries.never: exhort someone doing something, and exhort to someone. The object is bare and the complement is an infinitive.
entries.reports: urging delivered as rhetoric, to an audience rather than to a person — the verb of sermons, locker rooms, and commencement addresses. It is urge with an intended crowd, and unlike order it carries no power to compel: an exhortation can simply be ignored.
entries.see also: urge, call on, press, appeal to, push

entries.meaning: Contested — and the textbook rule has lost. Handbooks used to insist on forbid someone to do something and reject forbid someone from doing something as a confusion with prohibit. In current American English both are standard, from is if anything the more common in speech, and no mainstream usage guide still calls it an error. Write whichever reads better.
examples: Her father forbade her to see him again, which settled the matter in the other direction.
The lease forbids subletting for periods under thirty days.
Doctrine forbids members from taking an oath of any kind.
The coach forbade us to talk to reporters before the hearing.
Nothing in the bylaws forbids a board member from also being a vendor.
God forbid anyone actually reads the terms of service.
entries.русский: запрещать — личный запрет одного человека другому (родитель, начальник)
entries.patterns: forbid + sb + to-infinitive · forbid + sb + from + -ing · forbid + -ing (no person named: forbids smoking) · forbid + noun phrase · forbid + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: forbid someone doing something with no preposition. Either put from in or switch to the infinitive: forbade us from entering / forbade us to enter.
entries.forms: past forbade, traditionally /fərˈbæd/ · fer-BAD, though /fərˈbeɪd/ · fer-BAYD is now at least as common in American speech. Past participle forbidden. Forbid is also the one verb here whose God forbid survives as a fixed subjunctive.
entries.reports: a prohibition spoken by one person to another whom they have authority over — a parent, a boss, a commanding officer. Compare the institutional verbs:

examples: She implored the committee to hear one more witness.
His parents implored anyone who had seen the car to call the police.
I implore you to read the fine print this one time.
The doctor implored him to stop driving.
He implored her for a second chance and did not get one.
The letter implores the company not to close the last plant in the county.
entries.русский: умолять — самая эмоциональная мольба: отчаяние без утраты достоинства
entries.patterns: implore + sb + to-infinitive · implore + sb + for + noun phrase · implore + that-clause (rare, formal)
entries.never: implore to someone to do something, and implore someone from doing something.
entries.reports: the most emotionally charged of the pleading verbs — more intense than beg, less ritualized than beseech. It reports desperation without reporting loss of dignity, which is why journalists reach for it when quoting families of the missing.
entries.see also: beg, beseech, entreat, plead, appeal to

entries.meaning: Two verbs, split by mood. Insist leads a double life, and the mood of the that-clause is the only thing that separates a demand from an assertion: The directive sense never backshifts; the assertive sense backshifts normally, per Backshift, and is catalogued separately as insist. British writing renders the directive sense with should — insisted that he should be present — which is dialect, not error.
examples: She insisted on driving me to the airport at four in the morning.
He insisted on an itemized bill before he'd sign anything.
My grandmother insisted that everyone eat before the photographs.
They insisted on our being there an hour early, for no reason anyone explained.
The bank insists on two forms of identification.
He insisted that he had never met her, and the photographs said otherwise.
entries.русский: настаивать на — требовать повторно, уже получив отказ
entries.patterns: insist on + -ing · insist on + noun phrase · insist on + sb's + -ing (insisted on my paying) · insist on + sb + -ing (insisted on me paying — commoner in speech, still flagged by some editors) · bare insist + that-clause (subjunctive) · bare insist (intransitive: I insisted)
entries.never: insist someone to do something and insist on someone to do something — there is no infinitive frame in either shape. Repairs: insisted that I stay, insisted on my staying, insisted on paying.
entries.reports: a demand repeated against resistance. demand is a single act; insist implies the speaker has already been told no at least once and is not accepting it.

examples: The flight attendant instructed passengers to stow all loose items.
Her attorney instructed her to answer only the question asked.
The manual instructs you to disconnect the battery first.
He instructed the desk that no calls were to be put through.
She instructed us in how the filing system had been organized, which took an hour.
The pharmacist instructed him not to take it on an empty stomach.
entries.русский: инструктировать, поручать — деловое указание по процедуре, без эмоций
entries.patterns: instruct + sb + to-infinitive · instruct + that-clause (subjunctive) · instruct + sb + that-clause (informational) · instruct + sb + wh-clause (instructed us how to file it) · instruct + sb + in + noun phrase (= teach)
entries.never: instruct to fill out the form with no object, in the directive sense. Somebody is always instructed. And instruct someone doing something — there is no gerund frame.
entries.reports: a directive given as part of a procedure or a job — authority without emotion. A clerk instructs, a supervisor instructs, a lawyer instructs a client; none of them is angry. Compare tell, which is neutral but personal, and direct, which is one step more official.

examples: My parents never let me stay out past eleven.
Let me know when the car's out front.
She wouldn't let him pay for dinner.
They let the dog out at six every morning without fail.
He let the lease run out rather than argue about the deposit.
Don't let anyone tell you this was inevitable.
entries.русский: позволять, разрешать — бытовое разрешение; разг.; инфинитив без to
entries.patterns: let + sb + bare infinitive · let + sb + adverbial particle (let him in, let the dog out) · let's + bare infinitive (the first-person imperative)
entries.never: let someone to do something — no to, ever, in any tense. This is the single most reliable let error, and it comes from the fact that every neighboring verb (allow, permit, authorize) requires the to.
entries.no passive: ✗ He was let to leave and ✗ He was let leave are both impossible. Use He was allowed to leave. The only surviving passive is the fixed idiom be let go (= be fired), which is a different sense entirely.
entries.reporting let's: Let's leave is a proposal that includes the speaker, so it is reported with suggest or propose, never with tell: He suggested that we leave — never ✗ He suggested us to leave, and never ✗ He told us to leave, which reports an order instead.
entries.reports: permission in its most ordinary, domestic form — no institution, no paperwork, often no explicit request.

examples: Twenty-nine states mandate some form of paid sick leave.
The settlement mandates that the department publish quarterly data.
Federal law mandates a ninety-day notice period for plant closings.
The commission is mandated to report to the legislature each January.
Nothing in the charter mandates that meetings be held in person.
The district mandated masks for two weeks and then rescinded the rule.
entries.русский: предписывать в обязательном порядке — требование закона ко всем сразу; офиц.
entries.type: reporting verb — legal or institutional requirement
entries.patterns: mandate + that-clause (subjunctive) · mandate + noun phrase (mandates helmets) · passive be mandated to + infinitive (institutional)
entries.never: the law mandates employers to provide coverage — the active object plus infinitive is disfavored in edited American prose and flagged by usage panels. Repairs: mandates that employers provide coverage, mandates coverage. Note that the passive is mandated to is well established and unobjectionable: The agency is mandated to review every complaint.
entries.subjunctive: base form, no backshift — The ordinance mandated that every unit be inspected.
entries.reports: a requirement imposed by law, ordinance, or a governing body, on a whole class of people at once. Nobody mandates anything to an individual in conversation. Compare require, which is the same idea one register down and which happily takes the object plus infinitive.

examples: My roommate nagged me to return the library books until I finally did.
She nagged him about the smoke detector for a year, and then it went off at 3 a.m.
He nagged his way into a corner office and a reputation.
Stop nagging — I'll do it after lunch.
Something about the second paragraph kept nagging at me.
They nagged the city into repaving the block.
entries.русский: пилить, зудеть — разг.: надоедать бесконечно повторяемой просьбой
entries.patterns: nag + sb + to-infinitive · nag + sb + about + noun phrase · nag + sb + into + -ing · nag at + sb · nag (intransitive)
entries.never: nag someone that they should do something — no that-clause. And nag someone doing something without into.
entries.reports: requesting so often that the repetition itself has become the problem — the only verb in this group whose meaning includes the listener's reaction rather than the speaker's force. Reporting a request as nagging is an editorial verdict, and one that has historically been aimed at women far more than at men, which is worth knowing before you choose it in writing about a real person.

examples: The captain ordered the crew to abandon ship.
Her doctor ordered her to stay off the ankle for six weeks.
The court ordered that the company turn over its internal emails.
He ordered us out of the kitchen before the smoke alarm went off.
The agency ordered a recall of every lot from that plant.
Nobody ordered me to be here; I volunteered.
entries.русский: приказывать, велеть — обычное слово для властного распоряжения
entries.patterns: order + sb + to-infinitive · order + that-clause (subjunctive) · order + noun phrase (ordered a recount) · order + sb + adverbial particle (ordered him out)
entries.never: order to someone to do something — the addressee is a bare object. And order that he leaves — the that-clause takes the bare subjunctive, not the indicative.
entries.subjunctive: base form for every subject, and no backshift — The judge ordered that the records be sealed, not were sealed. The negative is plain not: ordered that the file not be released.
entries.negative infinitive: not goes in front of to — ordered us not to move, never ✗ ordered us to not move in edited prose.
entries.reports: the default word for an authoritative directive. Broader than command, which is military or absolute, and colder than tell, which is the same act reported without ceremony. A court, a doctor, a captain, and a parent can all order; only the first three sound natural doing it in a report.

examples: The permit permits excavation only between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m.
Her schedule doesn't permit a trip that long.
The museum does not permit flash photography in the print rooms.
Guests are permitted to use the pool until ten.
Weather permitting, the ceremony will be outdoors.
The evidence permits of no other reading.
entries.русский: разрешать — разрешение по правилам, в уставе или на табличке; офиц.
entries.patterns: permit + sb + to-infinitive · permit + -ing (no person named: permits smoking) · permit + noun phrase · passive be permitted to (very common) · permit of + noun phrase (formal: permits of no exception)
entries.never: permit that employees park here — permission takes no that-clause. Repairs: permits employees to park here, permits parking here.
entries.stress: the verb stresses the second syllable and the noun the first — the city won't perMIT it / you'll need a PERmit. This is the ordinary English noun–verb stress shift, and permit is one of its clearest cases.
entries.reports: institutional permission, stated in policies and posted on signs. Between let (domestic), allow (general), and authorize (a conferred power), permit is the one that belongs to rules.

examples: Residents petitioned the council to put a stoplight at the intersection.
He petitioned the state for reinstatement of his license.
Nineteen faculty members petitioned the dean to reverse the decision.
She petitioned the court to seal the juvenile records.
The union petitioned that the vote be conducted by secret ballot.
You can petition for a hardship waiver, but almost nobody gets one.
entries.русский: ходатайствовать, подавать петицию — офиц. письменное обращение к власти
entries.patterns: petition + sb + to-infinitive · petition + sb + for + noun phrase · petition for + noun phrase · petition + that-clause (subjunctive; legal)
entries.never: petition to the court to reopen the case — the addressee is a direct object, not the object of to. Repair: petitioned the court to reopen the case. (The noun does take to: a petition to the court.)
entries.reports: a request put to an authority in the form the authority requires — signatures, a filing, a formal letter. It reports the document as much as the utterance, which is why it is nearly always in the past tense and about groups.
entries.see also: request, appeal to, ask, call on, demand

examples: She pleaded with her brother to see a doctor.
The family pleaded for privacy after the verdict.
He pleaded with the officer not to write the ticket.
Neighbors pleaded with the city to slow traffic on the street for years.
He pleaded guilty to two counts and got probation.
She pleaded ignorance, unconvincingly.
entries.русский: умолять, упрашивать — долгая эмоциональная просьба; перед лицом нужен with
entries.patterns: plead with + sb + to-infinitive · plead for + noun phrase · plead with + sb + for + noun phrase · plead + noun phrase (pleaded ignorance, pleaded guilty — different senses) · plead + that-clause (= argue, a different sense)
entries.never: plead someone to do something — the preposition with is obligatory, and dropping it is one of the commonest errors in this file, because every neighbor (beg, implore, entreat, beseech) takes a bare object. Repair: pleaded with me to stay.
entries.past tense: pleaded is the form to write. Pled is extremely common in American speech and in courthouse usage, and no one will misunderstand it, but AP and most American style guides still print pleaded, including in pleaded guilty.
entries.reports: an appeal made over time and with visible emotion — longer than a beg, less formal than an appeal to. Note that the courtroom senses (plead guilty, plead the Fifth, plead a case) are separate verbs that report an entry on the record, not a request.
entries.see also: beg, implore, entreat, beseech, appeal to

examples: My advisor pressed me to submit before the fall deadline.
Reporters pressed the spokesman for a number and never got one.
The board is pressing for an outside audit.
She pressed him on the timeline until he admitted it had slipped.
They pressed us to sign that afternoon, which was itself a warning.
Nobody pressed the point, and the meeting moved on.
entries.русский: настойчиво добиваться, напирать — давить, не имея власти приказать
entries.patterns: press + sb + to-infinitive · press + sb + for + noun phrase · press + sb + on + noun phrase (pressed him on the timeline) · press for + noun phrase · press + noun phrase (pressed the point)
entries.never: press that someone do something — no that-clause of any kind. And press someone doing something. Repairs: pressed him to answer, pressed him for an answer.
entries.reports: persistent pushing toward an action or an answer, without the authority of order or the irritation of nag. It is the standard verb for a journalist who will not let a question go: Pressed on why the memo was never sent, she declined to answer.

examples: Federal law prohibits airlines from denying boarding on those grounds.
The lease prohibits subletting without written consent.
Our code of conduct prohibits accepting anything worth more than twenty-five dollars.
The injunction prohibited him from coming within five hundred feet of the school.
Nothing prohibits a nonprofit from lobbying; it just limits how much.
The rule prohibits the use of personal email for agency business.
entries.русский: запрещать — запрет, записанный в законе, правилах или договоре; офиц.
entries.patterns: prohibit + noun phrase · prohibit + -ing · prohibit + sb + from + -ing · prohibit + sb + from + noun phrase
entries.never: prohibit someone to do something — and unlike forbid, prohibit has no infinitive escape hatch at all. This is the sharpest structural line in the file: forbid takes either frame, prohibit takes only from + -ing. Repair: prohibits employees from accepting gifts.
entries.reports: prohibition written into a rule, a statute, a policy, or a lease — the prohibiting is done by the document, and the person who wrote it has usually vanished from the sentence. Compare forbid, where a person forbids another person.

entries.meaning: Often not a speech act at all. In most of its uses, the subject of prompt is an event rather than a speaker — The leak prompted an internal review. Only prompt someone to do something, with a human subject, reports an utterance; the rest reports causation.
examples: A whisper from the wings prompted him to pick up the line.
Her question prompted me to look at the numbers again.
The audit prompted a complete rewrite of the approval process.
The system prompts you for a second factor after ninety days.
He had to be prompted twice before he thanked anyone.
Nothing in the email prompted us to think it was urgent.
entries.русский: подсказать, подтолкнуть репликой — когда собеседник запнулся
entries.patterns: prompt + sb + to-infinitive · prompt + noun phrase (prompted an investigation) · prompt + sb + for + noun phrase (prompted him for the password) · prompt + sb + with + noun phrase
entries.never: prompt someone that they should do something — no that-clause. And prompt someone doing something.
entries.reports: the smallest directive in the file — one line, once, and only because the listener had stalled. An actor who forgets a line is prompted; so is a witness who needs the question repeated.

entries.meaning: Not prescribe. These two are near-opposites, they differ by one letter, and confusing them reverses the sentence:
examples: Most professional codes proscribe undisclosed conflicts of interest.
The regime proscribed the party and jailed its leadership.
Nothing in the guidelines proscribes citing preprints; they just discourage it.
Church law proscribed the practice for four centuries.
Grammar handbooks once proscribed the split infinitive, and nobody listened.
The treaty proscribes an entire class of weapon.
entries.русский: осуждать и запрещать — книжн.: объявлять недопустимым; не путать с prescribe
entries.type: reporting verb — formal condemnation and prohibition
entries.patterns: proscribe + noun phrase · proscribe + -ing
entries.never: proscribe someone to do something, and proscribe someone from doing something — the from frame that works so naturally with prohibit is not established here. Proscribe takes the forbidden thing as its object, not the person.
entries.reports: a formal denunciation that also forbids — historically, outlawing a person; now, ruling a practice out of bounds. It is the verb of style guides, professional codes, and academic writing about norms.

examples: Her parents pushed her to take the safer offer.
Two members of the board have been pushing for a change at the top since March.
He pushed me into buying the extended warranty and I've regretted it since.
Don't push him on it tonight; wait until he's slept.
The agency is pushing utilities to publish outage data.
Nobody pushed me; I wanted to go.
entries.русский: давить, продавливать — разг.: настойчиво склонять к решению в своих интересах
entries.patterns: push + sb + to-infinitive · push + sb + into + -ing · push for + noun phrase · push + sb + on + noun phrase
entries.never: push someone doing something without into, and push that someone do something — no that-clause.
entries.the into frame entails success: He pushed me into signing means I signed. He pushed me to sign leaves the outcome open. The same split runs through talk into, pressure into, and bully into.
entries.reports: repeated pressure toward a decision, with a strong hint that the person pushed was reluctant and the person pushing had an interest. It is press with the speaker's motives in view.

entries.meaning: Two frames, two speech acts. The infinitive reports a directive; the that-clause reports information. They are not interchangeable:
examples: Please remind me to move the car before street cleaning.
The dentist's office reminds you twice, by text and by phone.
She reminded the committee that the vote had already been taken once.
He reminded us of the last time somebody tried this.
Nobody reminded me the clocks changed, and I sat in an empty room for an hour.
Let me remind you who signed the check.
entries.русский: напоминать — побуждать к тому, что человек и сам раньше собирался сделать
entries.type: reporting verb — directive resting on prior intent
entries.patterns: remind + sb + to-infinitive · remind + sb + that-clause · remind + sb + of + noun phrase · remind + sb + about + noun phrase · remind + sb + wh-clause
entries.never: remind to bring your passport with no object — remind, like tell, always names the person. And remind someone doing something.
entries.reports: a directive whose whole force comes from the listener's own earlier intention — you can only be reminded to do something you had already meant to do. That presupposition is what separates it from tell: She told me to lock the door implies she decided; She reminded me to lock the door implies I had.

entries.meaning: The active object plus infinitive is stiff. We request you to complete the form is grammatical and reads like a form letter from 1955. American English strongly prefers the passive — Passengers are requested to remain seated — or the that-clause.
examples: He requested a copy of the inspection report in writing.
The court requested that both parties submit briefs by the tenth.
Guests are requested to keep noise down after ten.
She requested to be excused from the panel.
We request your presence at a reception following the ceremony.
The family has requested that donations go to the food bank instead of flowers.
entries.русский: просить официально — офиц., обычно письменно; «холодный» вариант ask
entries.patterns: request + noun phrase · request + that-clause (subjunctive) · request + to-infinitive (the subject acts: requested to be reassigned) · request + sb + to-infinitive (formal and stiff; the passive is the natural home)
entries.never: request for a copy as a verb — for belongs to the noun (a request for a copy), not the verb. Repair: requested a copy. And request someone something — ✗ requested him a copy.
entries.subjunctive: request that takes the base form and does not backshift: They requested that the session not be recorded, never ✗ that the session isn't recorded.
entries.reports: a request lodged in a formal register, usually in writing. It is ask with the temperature dropped: nobody requests a glass of water from a friend.
entries.see also: ask, demand, require, petition, call on

entries.meaning: The contrast with demand. These two mean nearly the same thing and behave differently, which is why the error migrates between them:
examples: The job requires you to be on call one weekend a month.
State law requires that landlords return deposits within twenty-one days.
The recipe requires buttermilk, and nothing else works the same way.
Employees are required to report outside income over five thousand dollars.
The grant requires filing a progress report every six months.
Nothing requires you to answer that question.
entries.русский: требовать — обязанность исходит от правила или условий, а не от человека
entries.patterns: require + that-clause (subjunctive) · require + sb + to-infinitive · require + noun phrase · require + -ing (requires wearing a badge) · passive be required to (the commonest form of all)
entries.never: require that every visitor signs in in American prose — the plain indicative in a directive that-clause is a British pattern and reads as an error in American writing. Repair: require that every visitor sign in. British English also has require that every visitor should sign in. Both British forms are dialect rather than error; neither belongs in American prose. What is impossible in either dialect is require someone doing something.
entries.reports: an obligation that comes from a rule, a policy, or the nature of the task rather than from a person's will. A person demands; a regulation requires. This is why require so often appears with an inanimate subject and in the passive: You are required to disclose it.

entries.meaning: Mood tells you what it is doing. Stipulate imposes a condition with the subjunctive and merely records a term with the indicative, and both are correct:
examples: The will stipulates that the house not be sold for ten years.
Her contract stipulates a minimum of four weeks' notice.
The grant stipulates how much can go to overhead.
They stipulated that neither side would discuss the settlement publicly.
The rules stipulate that entries be submitted electronically.
Both parties stipulated to the timeline, which saved a day of testimony.
entries.русский: оговаривать, предусматривать в договоре — юр.: условие, записанное на бумаге
entries.patterns: stipulate + that-clause · stipulate + noun phrase · stipulate + wh-clause (stipulates how the money may be spent) · stipulate to + noun phrase (courtroom sense — see below)
entries.never: stipulate someone to do something — no personal object before the complement. Repair: stipulated that he give thirty days' notice.
entries.second sense: in American courtrooms, stipulate also means to agree that a fact need not be proved — The parties stipulated to the authenticity of the emails. That sense takes to.
entries.reports: a requirement written into an agreement as a precondition of it — the difference from require is that a stipulation is negotiated, part of a bargain, and usually on paper.
entries.see also: require, mandate, decree, dictate, insist on

entries.meaning: Not summons. The noun is a summons (plural summonses). American legal usage also has a verb summons meaning "serve with a summons" — He was summonsed for failing to appear — which is a different word from summon and best left to lawyers.
examples: The principal summoned both students to her office before lunch.
He was summoned to testify and took the Fifth.
She summoned the waiter with a look that took about a second.
The board was summoned into an emergency session on a Sunday.
Someone finally summoned help from the road above.
Being summoned to headquarters is never good news.
entries.русский: вызывать — приказ явиться, которому нельзя не подчиниться; офиц., юр.
entries.patterns: summon + sb · summon + sb + to + noun phrase (summoned him to her office) · summon + sb + to-infinitive (summoned to appear) · summon + noun phrase (summoned help)
entries.never: summon someone that they come — no that-clause. And summon to someone — the person summoned is a direct object.
entries.reports: an order whose entire content is "come here" — the only verb in this group about location rather than action. The person summoned has no discretion; that is what distinguishes it from invite.
entries.see also: order, direct, command, call on, instruct

entries.meaning: Two verbs in one. Tell reports a command with an infinitive and a statement with a that-clause, and switching the frame switches the speech act: And say to is fine without an object. Textbooks say say cannot report a command; in real American speech He said to wait and She said not to bother are entirely normal. What is impossible is say with an object. To name the addressee, you must switch to tell.
examples: My boss told me to take the rest of the week off.
She told the kids not to open the door for anyone.
He told us that the flight had already been canceled.
Tell me what actually happened, not what's in the report.
Nobody told me the meeting had moved.
The sign tells you to stay on the trail, and people ignore it.
entries.русский: велеть, сказать сделать — с инфинитивом это приказ, с that-clause — сообщение
entries.type: reporting verb — command (also the general information verb)
entries.patterns: tell + sb + to-infinitive · tell + sb + that-clause · tell + sb + wh-clause · tell + sb + noun phrase (told me a story) · tell + sb + about + noun phrase
entries.never: tell to sit down and tell that he had left — tell always requires an object, in every one of its uses. And say someone to do something — its partner verb say refuses an object entirely. The object requirement is the sharpest line between the two.
entries.no subjunctive: unlike order and demand, tell does not license a mandative clause. ✗ He told that I leave is not English; the that-clause after tell is always an ordinary statement, backshifted per Backshift.
entries.reports: the plainest directive verb in the language — force-neutral, register-neutral, and by far the most common. Everything more specific in this file is tell plus an attitude.

examples: Her attorney urged her not to say anything publicly.
The Fed urged caution in a statement that moved nothing.
I'd urge you to read the dissent before making up your mind.
Public health officials urged residents to stay off the roads.
He urged that the matter be referred back to committee.
She urged me to apply, and I'm glad now that she did.
entries.русский: настоятельно советовать, призывать — сильно, но без власти принудить
entries.patterns: urge + sb + to-infinitive · urge + that-clause (subjunctive) · urge + noun phrase (urged caution) · urge + sb + on (a different sense: urged the horse on)
entries.never: urge to someone to do something, and urge someone doing something. The complement is an infinitive or a clause, never a gerund.
entries.subjunctive: urge that takes the base form and does not backshift — He urged that the vote be delayed.
entries.reports: a recommendation delivered with urgency by someone with no power to compel. It is the exact midpoint of this file: stronger than advise, weaker than demand, and unlike either, it says the speaker cared about the outcome. Officials and editorial boards urge; that is nearly all they can do.
entries.see also: press, push, exhort, call on, advise
